rationale: Section 8.1 sits at (and in places above) the fallback position: Commerce One expressly defends, indemnifies and holds Corio and its Customers harmless against third-party claims that the Software infringes patent, copyright, trademark or trade secret rights; the usual procedure (prompt notice, tender of control, cooperation) is present; and the remedy ladder is complete — procure the right to continue use, replace or modify, and failing those, terminate and refund a pro-rated portion of fees paid. The exclusions in Section 8.2 (use outside the Documentation; third-party modification) are within the permitted fallback exclusions and are in fact narrower than the fallback allows (no combination or specification carve-outs). No super-cap is needed because Section 9 expressly excludes "LIABILITY ARISING UNDER SECTION 8" from both the 12-month fees cap and the consequential-damages exclusion, leaving the indemnity uncapped — better for us than a 3x annual fees super-cap. There is no Corio indemnity anywhere in the Agreement, so there is no one-way exposure to narrow. Short of the preferred position, the indemnity does not extend to Commerce One's breach of applicable law, a Commerce One-caused data breach, or its gross negligence/wilful misconduct, and covers "Corio and its Customers" rather than affiliates; we note these as upside items only and do not redline a clause that meets the fallback on its material terms.

No element is merely promised in the margin comment. The deterministic 'Customer convenience termination present: false' signal is a false negative from alias matching. The operative sentence grants the right to "Corio", our client, and the drafter correctly avoided the defined term "CUSTOMER(S)" (§ 1.6 = Corio's sublicensees), which would have granted the exit to third parties. If Commerce One pushes back, the comment's offer to move to 60-90 days would still leave the fallback complete, since no early-termination fee exists and Commerce One has no convenience right. quote: 14.1 Assignment. Neither party may assign this Agreement or any rights or obligations hereunder, whether by operation of law or otherwise, without the prior written consent of the other party. Notwithstanding the foregoing, either party shall have the right to assign this Agreement in connection with the merger or acquisition of such party or the sale of all or substantially all of its assets related to this Agreement without such consent, except in the case where such transaction involves a direct competitor of the other party where consent of the other party will be required.
rationale: Section 14.1 is mutual and already carries an M&A/substantially-all-assets successor carve-out and a consent requirement for other assignments, so it is not walk-away territory (and no provision, including Sections 11.1-11.3, gives Commerce One any termination or re-pricing right on our change of control). It nevertheless fails the fallback on a material term: consent for non-successor assignments (and for a successor that is a direct competitor) may be withheld arbitrarily, with no reasonableness standard, and the successor route has no written notice mechanic. Our single edit inserts the "not unreasonably withheld" standard and a written notice requirement, bringing the clause to the fallback level; we have not pushed for the preferred asymmetric position (Corio affiliate assignment right and consent-only assignment by Commerce One), which remains available if the counterparty prefers to negotiate further.

verification.notes: Fallback is position-complete: the two insertions ("which consent shall not be unreasonably withheld" and "upon written notice to the other party") supply the only two fallback elements the original lacked, while mutual successor assignment and the consent requirement for other assignments were already present. Preferred is not reached: no Customer affiliate no-consent carve-out, and the competitor restriction is only a consent trigger rather than an absolute bar on Vendor assignment to a Customer competitor. To reach preferred the drafter would need to add an express Customer right to assign to an affiliate without consent and convert the competitor proviso into a flat prohibition on Vendor assignment to a Customer competitor. Minimality holds: no words were deleted, no survival tails, procedures, or extraneous obligations were added, and the reasonableness standard was placed on the existing consent sentence rather than by way of a broad notwithstanding override. Intent preserved: the direct-competitor consent proviso, the successors-and-permitted-assigns binding sentence, and the null-and-void remedy all survive without contradiction; no undefined terms or dangling cross-references are introduced. Classification as "deviation" is supportable — pre-edit the clause failed two material fallback terms (no reasonableness standard on consent, no notice mechanic) — though the gap was narrow and non-walk-away, since no Vendor change-of-control termination or re-pricing right appears.

We insert the fallback position only (E&O USD 1,000,000 and cyber/privacy USD 2,000,000), which is the shortest complete change; we did not volunteer the preferred CGL, workers' compensation or certificate mechanics.

verification.notes: Fallback checklist is complete: both the E&O USD 1,000,000 and cyber/privacy USD 2,000,000 limits are stated as affirmative, unconditional Vendor covenants ('shall maintain', 'not less than'), with the obligation correctly directed at Commerce One as Licensor/Vendor rather than at Corio. Preferred level fails on five of six elements: no CGL per-occurrence or aggregate limits, E&O set at 1M rather than 2M, cyber set at 2M rather than 5M, no workers' compensation covenant, and no certificates-on-request mechanic. To reach preferred the drafter must raise E&O to USD 2,000,000 and cyber to USD 5,000,000 and add CGL 1M/2M, statutory workers' compensation, and a certificate-on-request sentence. Minimality holds: the drafter omitted the model-language extras that are not in the chosen fallback checklist — 'at its own expense', the 'throughout the term and for one (1) year thereafter' survival tail, and the certificates mechanic — and inserted nothing beyond the two selected coverages. No existing words were deleted or paraphrased; §§14.9 and 14.10 are reproduced verbatim. Intent is preserved: the insertion is a standalone covenant in the miscellaneous section that creates no contradiction with the bankruptcy protection in 14.9 or the entire-agreement clause in 14.10, leaves no undefined term (it uses the defined party name Commerce One) and no dangling cross-reference. Minor drafting note only (not a defect against the checklist): the inserted paragraph carries the heading 'Insurance.' without a section number and sits between 14.9 and 14.10; renumbering it as 14.10 with consequent renumbering of Complete Understanding, or placing it after 14.10, would tidy the instrument. Detection status 'missing' is corroborated: the rationale confirms the only pre-existing use of 'insurance' is a net-revenue pricing deduction, so a concise insertion is the appropriate remedy for a hosting/licensing vendor.

rationale: Section 9 caps both parties (mutual) and mutually excludes indirect/consequential damages, and Section 8 (Indemnification) liability is expressly carved out of both the cap and the damages exclusion, so indemnities sit outside the cap. However the clause fails the fallback on two material terms: (i) the cap is not a true twelve-month fee cap because it is limited to amounts paid "FOR THE TRANSACTION WHICH THE LIABILITY RELATES TO", a subset that can fall well below twelve months' fees; and (ii) there are no carve-outs for breach of the Section 10 confidentiality obligations, gross negligence or wilful misconduct (searches return no such language anywhere in the document). Our redline is the shortest fallback-conforming fix: it deletes the per-transaction restriction and adds the three missing carve-outs to the existing exception opener, leaving all other wording verbatim. We have not pursued the preferred USD 1,000,000 floor, data-protection/security, fraud, IP-infringement or payment-obligation elements, which remain open if Commerce One will accept them.
ruleTitle: Limitation of liability — cap, mutuality and carve-outs

checks.name: cap references 12 months of fees or a fixed floor
no unlimited Customer liability language remains

elements.element: The aggregate liability cap applies mutually to both parties.
elements.evidence: Retained opener: "IN NO EVENT SHALL EITHER PARTY'S LIABILITY ARISING OUT OF THIS AGREEMENT OR THE USE OR PERFORMANCE OF THE SOFTWARE EXCEED..." — the cap binds both Corio (Customer) and Commerce One (Vendor); no unlimited-Customer-liability language remains.

elements.element: The cap is the greater of fees paid or payable in the 12 months preceding the claim and USD 1,000,000.
elements.evidence: As rendered the cap is "THE TOTAL AMOUNT ACTUALLY PAID BY CORIO HEREUNDER DURING THE TWELVE (12) MONTHS IMMEDIATELY PRIOR TO THE FILING OF THE CAUSE OF ACTION". There is no USD 1,000,000 alternative floor and no greater-of construction, and the basis is amounts "actually paid" rather than "paid or payable"; the temporal anchor is also filing of the cause of action rather than the event giving rise to the claim.

elements.element: The exclusion of indirect and consequential damages applies mutually to both parties.
elements.evidence: "IN NO EVENT SHALL EITHER PARTY HAVE ANY LIABILITY TO THE OTHER PARTY FOR ANY LOST PROFITS ... OR FOR ANY INDIRECT, SPECIAL OR CONSEQUENTIAL DAMAGES" — expressly bilateral and left unchanged.

elements.element: Breach of confidentiality obligations is uncapped.
elements.evidence: Inserted into the cap opener: "LIABILITY FOR BREACH OF SECTION 10 (CONFIDENTIALITY)" is excepted from the cap sentence; the confidentiality obligation exists in the document ("Each party hereby agrees that it shall not use any Confidential Information received from the other party...").

elements.element: Breach of data protection and security obligations is uncapped.
elements.evidence: The exception list is limited to Section 8, Section 10 (Confidentiality), gross negligence and wilful misconduct. No data protection or security carve-out appears anywhere in the rendered clause.

elements.element: Indemnification obligations are uncapped.
elements.evidence: Retained "EXCEPT FOR LIABILITY ARISING UNDER SECTION 8 OF THIS AGREEMENT"; Section 8.1 is the indemnification provision ("Commerce One shall indemnify, defend and hold harmless Corio..."), so indemnity liability sits outside both the cap and the consequential-damages exclusion.

elements.element: Gross negligence is uncapped.
elements.evidence: Inserted: "AND LIABILITY ARISING FROM A PARTY'S GROSS NEGLIGENCE OR WILLFUL MISCONDUCT" precedes the cap language, so gross negligence is excepted from the cap.

elements.element: Fraud is uncapped.

elements.element: The aggregate liability cap applies mutually to both parties.

verification.notes: The redline is position-complete at the fallback level: mutual cap, true twelve-month fee basis, and carve-outs for indemnification (existing Section 8), confidentiality, gross negligence and wilful misconduct. Preferred level is not reached: no greater-of USD 1,000,000 floor, "paid" rather than "paid or payable", no data protection/security, fraud or other-party-IP carve-outs, and no statement that Customer's payment obligations are outside the cap. To reach preferred the drafter must (i) recast the cap as "the greater of the fees paid or payable by Corio in the twelve (12) months immediately preceding the event giving rise to the claim and USD 1,000,000", (ii) add data protection/security, fraud and infringement of the other party's IP to the exception list, and (iii) add an express sentence that Corio's obligation to pay fees is not subject to the cap. Minimality holds: only two edits were made inside the target clause — deletion of the per-transaction narrowing ("FOR THE TRANSACTION WHICH THE LIABILITY RELATES TO") and insertion of three carve-outs into the existing exception opener. No survival tail, expense language, extra damages categories or boilerplate were added, and the favourable mutual consequential-damages sentence and the risk-allocation sentence were retained verbatim. Intent is preserved: the Section 8 indemnity carve-out, the bilateral exclusion of lost profits and indirect/special/consequential damages, and the reasonable-allocation-of-risk acknowledgement all survive without contradiction; the inserted cross-reference is self-identifying ("SECTION 10 (CONFIDENTIALITY)") and matches the confidentiality obligation in the document, leaving no dangling reference. If the confidentiality obligation is not in fact numbered Section 10, the drafter should conform the numbering before circulation. The removed per-transaction limiter was Vendor-favourable narrowing of the cap, so its deletion is a permitted target-element change, not removal of Customer-favourable language.
